newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: ANALYSTS SEE GLITTERING DE BEERS H1 RESULTS.
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS SEE GLITTERING DE BEERS H1 RESULTS.

text.p: Diamond giant De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd is set to post sparkling first half results next week on the back of increased diamond sales and a weaker South African rand, analysts said on Friday.
De Beers and its international arm, De Beers Centenary AG, report combined results for the half year to end-June, 1997, on Tuesday.
Analysts said the main reason for the expected increase in results would be the weaker South African rand and increased sales from De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation (CSO).
"We've got a pretty good indication of the underlying health of the diamond business (which) came out of the CSO sales which went to an all-time record," said BOE Natwest analyst Barry Sergeant.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast net attributable earnings to increase to between $510 million and $543 million from $482 million -- excluding earnings from associates -- a year ago.
"It will be a nice healthy increase," Sergeant said.
CSO diamond sales in the first half of the financial year increased 4.8 percent to $2.88 billion. Analysts said they expected CSO year sales to top $5 billion in the full year.

G O'Flaherty analyst Des Mayers and Investec Securities analyst Hennie Vermeulen said they expected De Beers to post an increase in headline earnings of around 22 percent on the same period last year.
Mayers and Sergeant said earnings would somewhat be distorted by the proceeds of the sale of De Beers' stake in JCI Ltd to a black empowerment consortium earlier this year.
"It is going to be severely distorted by a number of one-offs, for example bringing in some of the profits of the sale of JCI," Sergeant said.
He said that he expected De Beers' diamond account -- profit from mining and trading diamonds -- to be up 6.2 percent in dollar terms from $447 million in the half year to end-June 1996.
Industry sources said De Beers might express some concern at reduced demand for diamonds from the Japanese retail sector.
The analysts said they expected De Beers to sign a long-delayed gem trade deal with Russia soon.
De Beers has cut the amount of diamonds it purchased from Russia's monopoly diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS) at the end of 1996 after the government failed to approve a trade deal.
Russia and De Beers has been without a deal since December 1995, when the last trade agreement expired.
